survey: A single upright headstone in grey stone. The slab has an arched top and stands in the middle of a wider rectangular plinth, which rests flat on a grey ledge and casts a shadow to the left. A raised cross is carved in relief in the upper centre of the front face. A zig-zag crack starts at a notch in the top-right shoulder and runs about halfway down the face, then stops. At that notch the arch ends in a vertical face with stacked step-like ledges. Below it, the right part of the slab carries on at a lower height with its own neatly rounded corner. Moss clumps cling to the top-left edge and to the bottom-left corner where the slab meets the plinth. A small orange flower with a green stem lies flat on the plinth at the front right. The slab faces the camera in three-quarter view, with its right side face visible.

errors.where: Top-right shoulder of the slab, at the notch where the crack starts
errors.what: The break does not make physical sense. The right part of the slab sits lower than the arch, as if it had slid down. Yet the crack is only a shallow groove that stops halfway down, so that part is still solid with the slab and could not have dropped. The notch is built from neat stacked steps, and the lower part has a smooth rounded corner of its own. A fracture would leave a jagged, uneven edge on one continuous outline. What we see reads as two different headstone outlines merged into one.

fix: One continuous slab with a single smooth arched top running from the left edge to the right edge. Show the damage as a chipped piece missing from the top-right corner, with a rough, jagged broken edge. Start the zig-zag crack inside that chipped area and run it down the face. No stepped ledges and no lower second shoulder: the right side keeps the same height and outline as the rest of the arch.
